primitives.name: Compound Conditioning Principle
primitives.verbatim_quote: 398 PRINCIPLES OF BEHAVIOR learning is that in which a stimulus compound is conditioned to evoke a reaction while the several components when acting alone are consistently extinguished.
primitives.assumptions: Stimulus components are independently ineffective; compound induces response through synergistic interaction.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When S_i components act alone, R approaches zero due to extinction.

layer2.mapping: GSI: Conditional probability P(R|S_c) > P(R|S_i) for all i; GSE: State transition S_c → R with S_i → ∅
layer2.telemetry: Response rate under compound vs. component stimuli

The Compound Conditioning Principle defines a core behavioral mechanism where a composite stimulus elicits a response not achievable by individual components alone. This implies a non-linear synergy in perception-action systems, enabling complex behaviors from simple inputs. The Primary Principle Isolation establishes a foundational axiomatic structure, suggesting that all observable behavior can be logically deduced from a small set of fundamental laws—this mirrors the emergence of higher-order theories from basic physical principles. The Scientific Formulation Certainty supports an iterative refinement approach, where initial imperfect models accelerate convergence toward truth. These primitives form a triadic system: foundational laws (P_n), emergent complexity (S_c → R), and epistemic evolution (F → C). Dualities emerge between deterministic causality and probabilistic inference, with failure modes including overfitting to component data and underestimating synergistic effects. The breakdown regimes reveal critical thresholds in both model clarity and behavioral complexity.
